questions.question: The three possible measuring points on the circular flow are:
options: PRODUCTION, INCOME and SPENDING — three gauges on one pipe, in principle one total

questions.question: GDP is defined as:
options: All money that changed hands in a country during a year
The total market value of all FINAL goods and services produced WITHIN a country's borders in a given period
The income of a country's citizens wherever they live
The value of everything a country's shops sold

questions.question: GDP is expressed in MARKET VALUE so that:
options: Unlike things — haircuts and coal trucks — can be added into one total

questions.question: "In a given period" marks GDP as:
options: A FLOW per year — production during the period, not an accumulated pile

subtopics.title: GDP's Fine Print — Final Goods and the Border

questions.question: Fleece sold for R30, yarn for R70, jersey for R200. GDP counts:
options: R200 — the final jersey only; fleece and yarn are intermediate goods already inside its price

questions.question: The VALUE ADDED at each wool stage is:
options: Farmer R30, mill R40, knitter R130 — summing to the same R200

questions.question: The Australian-owned mine on South African soil counts in:
options: SOUTH AFRICAN GDP — produced within our borders, whoever banks the dividends

questions.question: Excluded from GDP, with reason:
options: New machinery — too expensive to count
Teachers' salaries — services do not count
Second-hand sales, share shuffles, grants and most unpaid work — none creates NEW production (though a dealer's service fee counts)

questions.question: The single contrast between GDP and GNI:
options: GDP asks WHERE production happened; GNI asks WHO earned the income — geography versus ownership
GDP counts goods; GNI counts services
GDP is yearly; GNI is monthly
GDP includes government; GNI excludes it

questions.question: The bridge from GDP to GNI runs:
options: GDP plus all exports minus all imports
GDP MINUS factor payments to the rest of the world PLUS factor income received from it

questions.question: South Africa's GNI sits somewhat below its GDP because:
options: Substantial foreign ownership means more factor income leaves than arrives — the machine here produces more than residents keep

questions.question: Lesotho showing GNI ABOVE GDP tells us:
options: Its territory produces more than its people earn
Many citizens work abroad and remit wages — its PEOPLE earn more than its TERRITORY produces

subtopics.title: Per Capita, Comparisons and the Limits of the Number

questions.question: GDP PER CAPITA is used because:
options: Totals mislead when populations differ — dividing by population gives output per person, the first correction for welfare comparisons

questions.question: Comparing this year's GDP with last year's also requires:
options: Stripping out the inflation effect — a bigger number is no better if prices merely rose

questions.question: "One tycoon and ninety-nine unemployed still average out respectably" exposes GDP's blindness to:
options: DISTRIBUTION — the number is silent on who holds the income

questions.question: "A speedometer, not a report card" means GDP:
options: Reads how fast the economy produces — but not how well people live, for whom, or at what cost to the future

questions.question: The panel beater buys parts for R400 and returns the car for R1 500. The street's count includes:
options: R1 500 once — or equivalently his R1 100 of added skill; adding the parts sale too would double-count

questions.question: The neighbour selling his old bakkie is excluded because:
options: It was counted the year it was built — today money moved but nothing NEW was made

questions.question: The bottle store owned by a man from the next town counts in the street's total because:
options: The border rule counts what is made ON the street — it stands here, hires here, produces here

questions.question: Under the WHERE-rule (GDP), the street's daughter working in Cape Town:
options: Does NOT count — her production happens there, not on this street

questions.question: Under the WHO-rule (GNI), the same daughter:
options: COUNTS — she is the street's resident and her salary flows home

questions.question: "Big GDP, smaller GNI — the machine is here, the keeping is elsewhere" describes:
options: Roughly South Africa's shape — significant foreign ownership sends profits out at closing time

questions.question: The real story told by comparing a country's GDP and GNI lies in:
options: Whichever number is larger being the true one
The GAP between them — it reveals who owns the machine and where the earnings go

subtopics.title: What the Big Number Can't See

questions.question: The street produced R2 million but one household banked R1,8 million. GDP's blind spot here is:
options: DISTRIBUTION — the total is not a sharing; the average hides the split

questions.question: The grandmother minding four grandchildren daily illustrates:
options: Untilled work — real production the official number never sees, understating economies like ours

questions.question: Selling the old jacaranda for firewood RAISES the count because:
options: Firewood is exempt from the border rule
GDP records the timber revenue but not the lost tree — production that eats tomorrow looks identical to production that does not

questions.question: "Count carefully; question the count" asks you to hold both truths:
options: GDP is meaningless and should be scrapped
GDP is the complete measure of welfare
The number matters — growth funds wages, taxes and clinics — AND it is a speedometer, silent on how well, for whom, and at what cost
